item.title: Rapid7: Webworm hides SoftEther VPN Bridge behind NtMonitor branding, new endpoints and an encrypted config
item.description: Rapid7 describes NtMonitor, a Windows build of SoftEther VPN Bridge 4.44 that it attributes with moderate confidence to Webworm, the China-aligned actor that ESET documented moving to European government targets in May 2026. The rebuild keeps SoftEther's function of bridging a remote network into the victim's LAN and strips its fingerprints: branding, handshake paths, the handshake watermark, the separate resource archive and the plain-text configuration are all changed, and Rapid7 found no backdoor or other added capability. Only one antivirus vendor detected the sample on VirusTotal although it has been public since January.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB3

Webworm's NtMonitor: Rapid7 finds a custom rebuild of the SoftEther VPN Bridge that removes the open-source tool's detection fingerprints (rebranded metadata, renamed handshake endpoints, a custom handshake watermark, an embedded resource archive and an encrypted configuration), attributed with moderate confidence to the China-aligned actor that targets European governments

Rapid7 analysed what it believes is a so-far unknown custom tool, a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge version 4.44 (build 9807) that it attributes to Webworm with moderate confidence (Rapid7, 2026-11-19). Webworm is the China-aligned actor that ESET reported in May 2026 moving to European government targets and to dual-use tools such as SoftEther (ESET Research, 2026-05-20). The rebuild keeps the bridge function, which cascades a remote network into the victim's local network, and removes the fingerprints: the PE metadata and internal strings are rebranded as a network-monitoring product (inconsistently, since the service name and many registry paths still say SoftEther), the HTTP handshake endpoints get update-style names, the handshake watermark becomes a truncated PNG header so stock SoftEther peers cannot connect and the stock watermark cannot fingerprint the build, the resource archive that normally sits beside the executable is embedded in it as a PE resource, and the configuration is stored under a new name in a custom-encrypted format (Rapid7, 2026-11-19). Rapid7 found no backdoor or other added capability, concludes the actor puts stealth above capability, and says only one antivirus vendor detected the sample although it has been public since January (Rapid7, 2026-11-19).

Exposure
Windows hosts in government networks that Webworm has already compromised; Rapid7 says that in every configuration it holds the VPN is set to bridge a remote network into the local one (Rapid7, 2026-11-19).
Detection
Rapid7's most reliable network detection, where TLS traffic can be inspected, is a POST request to an update-themed CGI path with a JPEG content type whose body starts with a PNG file header; on hosts, look for a SoftEther VPN Bridge service that was not installed by the organisation, in particular one whose binary carries its resource archive inside itself, and for firewall rules added by such a service (Rapid7, 2026-11-19). Rapid7 calls the branding the easiest change for the actor to make next and says the endpoints and watermark can be swapped out trivially, so behaviour that is intrinsic to SoftEther matters more than any one string (Rapid7, 2026-11-19).
Defender takeaway
Government networks in Europe should treat any unmanaged SoftEther VPN Bridge, however it is named, as a persistence mechanism that bridges an outside network into theirs, and learn the tool's intrinsic behaviour, as Rapid7 recommends for the government sector (Rapid7, 2026-11-19).

item.title: Hokkaido: municipal data on a subcontractor's PC hit by K2F stealer via a game launcher; Rumoi's contract had ended
item.description: On 2026-11-18 and 2026-11-19 the Hokkaido municipalities Iwamizawa, Rumoi and Shintoku disclosed that data they gave their contractor GIS Hokkaido was stored on a development terminal of its subcontractor Rimgate that the K2F information stealer infected overnight on 2 to 3 November: up to 71,002 resident-register and 4,503 support-needed records for Rumoi, whose personal data was still on the terminal after its contract ended, 6,001 resident-register and 986 evacuation-support records for Shintoku, and fixed-asset-tax land and building data for Iwamizawa. GIS Hokkaido told ITmedia that the PC launcher of the game NIKKE is involved and would not say whether Rimgate staff ran the game on the work PC; no leak or misuse is confirmed, and none of the data contains the national My Number.
item.content:encoded:
ROUTINENATOA2

Hokkaido: resident-register, support-needed and tax data of the cities of Rumoi and Iwamizawa and the town of Shintoku sat on a subcontractor's development PC infected with the K2F information stealer, which GIS Hokkaido links to the NIKKE game launcher; Rumoi's data was still there after its contract ended

Three Hokkaido municipalities disclosed on 2026-11-18 and 2026-11-19 that personal data they had handed to their contractor GIS Hokkaido was stored on a development terminal of GIS Hokkaido's subcontractor Rimgate, on which traces of the information stealer K2F were found: the terminal was infected overnight on 2 to 3 November, Rimgate found the traces on 4 November and cut it from the network, and GIS Hokkaido told the municipalities between 13 and 16 November (Rumoi City, 2026-11-19; Iwamizawa City, 2026-11-18; Shintoku Town, 2026-11-18). The data at risk is up to 71,002 resident-register records (as of February 2022) and 4,503 records of people needing support, with disability category and care level, for Rumoi, whose personal data was still on the terminal after its contract ended; 6,001 resident-register and 986 disaster-evacuation-support records for Shintoku; and up to 10,348 land parcels and 7,037 buildings of fixed-asset-tax data for Iwamizawa; none contains the national My Number and no leak or misuse is confirmed (translated from Japanese) (Rumoi City, 2026-11-19; Iwamizawa City, 2026-11-18; Shintoku Town, 2026-11-18). GIS Hokkaido told ITmedia that the PC launcher of the game NIKKE is involved and declined to say whether Rimgate staff ran the game on the work PC; ITmedia adds that a third-party tampering with that launcher, which could deliver K2F on start, became public on 5 November (translated from Japanese) (ITmedia NEWS, 2026-11-19). This is municipal public-sector data held through a supplier chain.

Exposure
Any administration whose resident, social-care or tax data went to a contractor that subcontracts, and any supplier endpoint where consumer software such as a game launcher can run next to project data; the check is which supplier terminals still hold extracts from finished projects (Rumoi City, 2026-11-19; ITmedia NEWS, 2026-11-19).
Detection
The infection path is the observable: a consumer game launcher on a workstation that holds project data, and, because K2F steals passwords and allows remote control, password-store reads by non-browser processes and unexplained remote sessions on such machines; the sources give no more specific indicator (ITmedia NEWS, 2026-11-19).
Defender takeaway
Ask each supplier and its subcontractors which of your extracts they still hold, have them delete data of finished contracts and confirm it, and keep consumer software off the machines that handle it; Rumoi's contract had ended yet its data was still on the infected terminal (Rumoi City, 2026-11-19).

item.title: Basel-Landschaft: attackers took about 97,000 cross-border work-permit records; no entry point or actor named
item.description: On 2026-11-20 the canton of Basel-Landschaft said that forensic analysis by external experts confirmed the attackers reached a database of work permits for cross-border commuters (permit G) and took data from it: about 97,000 records from applications lodged through its online platform since 2016-11-28, with names, addresses, birth dates, nationality, occupation, the ZEMIS identification number and employers' contact details. The canton cannot say which records left and assumes all did; it names no entry point, tool or actor, took the platform off the network and filed a criminal complaint against unknown persons.
item.content:encoded:
ROUTINENATOA2

Canton Basel-Landschaft: attackers took about 97,000 records from a database of work permits for cross-border commuters (permit G) in the cyberattack on the cantonal administration; the canton cannot say which records, assumes all, and names no entry point or actor

A confirmed data theft from a Swiss cantonal administration: the canton of Basel-Landschaft said on 2026-11-20 that forensic analysis showed the attackers reached a database of work permits for cross-border commuters (permit G) and took about 97,000 records for applications lodged through its online platform since 2016-11-28 (Canton Basel-Landschaft, 2026-11-20). It cannot establish which records were taken and assumes all, took the platform off the network, filed a criminal complaint against unknown persons and names no entry point, tool or actor (Canton Basel-Landschaft, 2026-11-20; Polizeiticker, 2026-11-20), after other cantonal applications had been switched off earlier in the week (Inside IT, 2026-11-20).

Exposure
Persons for whom a permit-G application was lodged, renewed or changed through the cantonal platform since 2016-11-28, and the contact persons of their employers in the canton; the database kept completed procedures too, so people whose permits ended are affected as well (Canton Basel-Landschaft, 2026-11-20). The canton cannot exclude that uploaded documents such as contracts or ID copies were taken but has no indication of it (Canton Basel-Landschaft, 2026-11-20).
Defender takeaway
An online application platform that keeps every historic procedure puts the whole archive in play when it is reached, so check how much completed data your own citizen-facing and supplier-run platforms retain; employers of cross-border commuters in the canton should expect phishing and social engineering that quotes correct personal details, because the canton warns that such messages can be built from the stolen data (Canton Basel-Landschaft, 2026-11-20).

item.title: Update: Zammad 6.5.5 emergency-fixes the exploited session-leak RCE on 6.5; 7.2.3 now supersedes 7.2.2 (root escalation)
item.description: DIVD completed its forensic investigation: the attacker, who used AI agents after reaching root, was mainly after credentials (a GitLab token, a Slack key and shared-mailbox OAuth tokens); about 41,000 ticket titles and a limited set of older conversations left the host, and the first response started 19 hours after the alert. Zammad's release 7.2.3 of 2026-11-11, a critical security update, supersedes 7.2.2 as the build to install.
item.content:encoded:
Update20 Nov 2026 05:14 UTCrun 2026-11-20T0356Z-inteltechniquessourcesbodycvesactionsheadlinesummary

DIVD completed its forensic investigation: the attacker, who used AI agents after reaching root, was mainly after credentials (a GitLab token, a Slack key and shared-mailbox OAuth tokens); about 41,000 ticket titles and a limited set of older conversations left the host, and the first response started 19 hours after the alert. Zammad's release 7.2.3 of 2026-11-11, a critical security update, supersedes 7.2.2 as the build to install.

DIVD completed its forensic investigation and updated its case file on 2026-11-18 (DIVD, 2026-11-18). It says that after obtaining root the attacker used AI agents to continue the attack, which it infers from the volume of payloads and the comments in the attack scripts (DIVD, 2026-11-18), and that the attacker was mainly interested in credentials, all of which have been rotated (DIVD, 2026-11-18). The credential material it touched was a GitLab personal access token that could not reach the internal GitLab, a Slack API key without read permission and the OAuth tokens of two shared mailboxes, used to send test emails with no mailbox-content compromise observed; only the host carrying Zammad was compromised at root level, and because direct outbound traffic from it was impossible the extraction from the ticket system was selective, about 41,000 ticket titles and a limited set of older conversations (DIVD, 2026-11-18); DIVD says its Jira and Confluence environment was also compromised, with 207 volunteer email addresses, two phone numbers and seven profile pictures taken (DIVD, 2026-11-18). DIVD says its alert arrived quickly but it took 19 hours to initiate the first response, and that there is plenty of room for improvement (DIVD, 2026-11-18). Separately, Zammad released 7.2.3 on 2026-11-11 as a critical security update that addresses several vulnerabilities, so 7.2.2 is no longer the build to install, and it requires an nginx or Apache2 configuration change that clears the Remote-User header next to X-Forwarded-User, which the Docker images apply automatically (Zammad, 2026-11-11).

Open finding: CVE-2026-102489 / CVE-2026-102490, Zammad helpdesk: a session-hijack remote code execution and a zammad-to-root escalation, both reported exploited since 21 September; 7.2.2 fixes the root flaw on DEB and RPM installs →

item.title: Update: FBI: various actors run ARTEX against many sectors, government included; Microsoft names Storm-0940 and Storm-3358
item.description: The European Commission confirmed an AI-generated cyber campaign against its internal systems, which it says it detected on 2026-10-22, with its HR and medical-reimbursement systems disrupted for more than 10 days per POLITICO; only an anonymous EU official names ARTEX, POLITICO places CERT-EU's finding of ARTEX use at a different date, and no access vector is stated.
item.content:encoded:
Update20 Nov 2026 05:12 UTCrun 2026-11-20T0356Z-intelsourcesbody

The European Commission confirmed an AI-generated cyber campaign against its internal systems, which it says it detected on 2026-10-22, with its HR and medical-reimbursement systems disrupted for more than 10 days per POLITICO; only an anonymous EU official names ARTEX, POLITICO places CERT-EU's finding of ARTEX use at a different date, and no access vector is stated.

The European Commission confirmed on 2026-11-19 that an AI-generated cyber campaign hit its internal systems: its spokesperson said the incident was detected on 2026-10-22 and confirmed on 2026-10-26, that several applications were taken offline as a protective measure and most are restored, that there is no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole and that it is not aware of a ransom request, and the Commission names no tool or attacker and declines to attribute or size the campaign (European Commission, 2026-11-19). POLITICO, citing an anonymous EU official, reports that CERT-EU detected earlier this month that international hackers used ARTEX, that the staff HR platform Sysper and the medical-reimbursement system MyPMO were disrupted for more than 10 days, and that investigators have not yet established whether staff data was compromised (POLITICO, 2026-11-19). The dates differ: the Commission says detection was on 2026-10-22, while POLITICO's official places CERT-EU's finding of ARTEX use earlier in November, and the sources do not reconcile them. The Commission has not confirmed the ARTEX link (European Commission, 2026-11-19), and the reporting does not establish whether ARTEX provided entry or was only used to find weaknesses (Cyber Security News, 2026-11-19).

Open finding: ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration →

item.content:encoded:

ReversingLabs' follow-up adds hunting specifics to Cereal, now in the Detection line: the loaders appear under other vendor names (BlankPage, CerealMood), a check for live HTTP.sys listeners, the proxy-DLL names to look for in Exchange and Windows service directories and module loads in WmiPrvSE.exe; it adds no victim or entry vector.

ReversingLabs correlated ESET's published loader samples and says the same files carry different vendor names, CerealLoader at ESET, BlankPage in Microsoft Defender and CerealMood in other engines, so a hunt on a single family name can miss matches; it says the work extends the artifacts defenders can search for and establishes no additional victims or initial-access method (ReversingLabs, 2026-11-19). Its hunting guidance (HTTP.sys listeners, proxy-DLL loaders such as version.dll and WTSAPI32.dll, and WmiPrvSE.exe module loads) is in the Detection line (ReversingLabs, 2026-11-19).

item.title: USI Lugano: forms system exploited 9 to 17 November; mainly contact data, 8,000+ warning e-mails sent
item.description: The Swiss university USI said on 2026-11-19 (communiqué translated from Italian) that unauthorised third parties had access to data on one of its applications between 2026-11-09 and 2026-11-17 by exploiting a vulnerability in the software of an online-forms system that collects job applications, scholarship requests and surveys. The server held the form responses and their attached documents; USI secured it and informed the authorities and the people concerned. Its chief operating officer said on 2026-11-20 that the stolen data are mainly names, e-mail addresses and phone numbers, with a small share of job applications and scholarship requests, that more than 8,000 e-mails warned those concerned, and that AI agents found and exploited the flaw, which is USI's own assessment with no technical evidence given. USI names no product, vulnerability or attacker, and no extortion claim has been reported.
item.content:encoded:

Università della Svizzera italiana (USI, Lugano): third parties exploited a vulnerability in an online-forms system and had access to form responses and attached documents from 9 to 17 November 2026, mainly contact details, and more than 8,000 e-mails warned those concerned; USI names no product or actor

USI said on 2026-11-19 that unauthorised third parties had access to data held on one of its applications between 2026-11-09 and 2026-11-17, by exploiting a vulnerability in the software of an online-forms system that the university uses to collect certain job applications, scholarship requests and surveys (USI via Corriere del Ticino, 2026-11-19). The affected server held the responses to the forms and their attached documents; USI's IT services secured it, USI informed the competent authorities and the people whose data may be affected, and it says the causes and the risk to those concerned are still being checked, which will take several more weeks (USI via laRegione, 2026-11-19). It names no product, vulnerability or attacker, and Ticinonline adds that it is not yet clear when the intrusion began or how long it lasted (Ticinonline, 2026-11-19).

Defender takeaway
Check any forms, survey or application-intake system, your own or a supplier's, that stores uploaded documents, and treat those documents as exposed on a system that was reachable with vulnerable software during the access window of 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-17 (USI via laRegione, 2026-11-19).

item.title: Mitel OpenScape 4000: two unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 Platform flaws; upgrade to V11 R2.14 or restrict access
item.description: Mitel's advisory MISA-2026-0013 of 2026-11-18 covers three flaws in the Platform component of OpenScape 4000 and OpenScape 4000 Manager: an unauthenticated improper-authentication flaw and an unauthenticated command injection, both CVSS 3.1 10.0, and a command injection reachable from the adjacent network (9.6). CVE ids have been requested but not assigned; the fix is V11 R2.14, PLT HF5 on V11 R1.26 or a patch for V10 R0.28 to V11 R0.22, and enabling Security Mode restricted access is Mitel's workaround. The advisory says nothing about exploitation, and it is the second critical Mitel advisory in a week.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOA2

Mitel OpenScape 4000 and OpenScape 4000 Manager, MISA-2026-0013: two unauthenticated flaws in the Platform component rated CVSS 3.1 10.0 (improper authentication, command injection) and an adjacent-network command injection (9.6); CVE ids pending, fixed in V11 R2.14, Security Mode restricted access is the workaround, no exploitation stated

Mitel's advisory MISA-2026-0013 of 2026-11-18 covers three flaws in the Platform component of OpenScape 4000 and OpenScape 4000 Manager, tracked by Mitel's internal ids because the CVE identifiers it requested are not yet assigned (Mitel, 2026-11-18). MTLVULN-1785 is an unauthenticated improper-authentication flaw that gives unauthorized access and MTLVULN-1786 an unauthenticated command injection through insufficient parameter sanitization, both CVSS 3.1 10.0 with changed scope; MTLVULN-1793 is a command injection that an unauthenticated attacker with adjacent network access can use, scored 9.6 (Mitel, 2026-11-18). Affected are OpenScape 4000 V11 R0.22 through V11 R2.11 and V10 R1.68 and earlier, and OpenScape 4000 Manager V11 R0.22 through V11 R2.11 and V10 R1.34, R1.42, R1.54 and R1.68; Mitel does not assess end-of-support releases (Mitel, 2026-11-18).

The issues are corrected in V11 R2.14, Mitel provides PLT HF5 for V11 R1.26 and a patch for V10 R0.28 to V11 R0.22 (for the Manager, V10 R1.34 to V11 R0.22), and for customers who cannot apply the fix quickly, enabling Security Mode restricted access is a workaround that prevents exploitation, with the steps in a portal-only article (Mitel, 2026-11-18). CERT-FR lists the risks as remote arbitrary code execution, remote denial of service, policy bypass and loss of integrity and confidentiality, and BSI describes an attacker who can bypass safeguards, disclose information or run arbitrary commands in the context of the system (CERT-FR, 2026-11-19; BSI, 2026-11-19). Mitel's text does not mention exploitation.

Exposure
OpenScape 4000 and OpenScape 4000 Manager at the releases above; the vulnerable component is the Platform, and the advisory does not say which of its interfaces are normally reachable (Mitel, 2026-11-18).
Detection
Unauthenticated access to the Platform component from hosts that are not administration or maintenance systems, and unexpected command execution on the platform; both follow from the improper-authentication and command-injection mechanisms, and the advisory gives no detection guidance.
Defender takeaway
Apply the fix for the release in use now; where that waits, turn on Security Mode restricted access, and read the affected range against CERT-FR's wording if the system runs R2.12 or R2.13 (Mitel, 2026-11-18; CERT-FR, 2026-11-19).

item.title: Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13, 3.3.14 fix seven memory flaws; a Rails exploit is announced for 25 November: update the interpreter
item.description: The Ruby project released 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 on 2026-11-18 for seven memory-corruption flaws in the regexp engine and in string case conversion, three rated Critical, and says it knows of proofs of concept that reach remote code execution. Veria Labs, which found the case-conversion flaw independently (CVE-2026-132825, a one-byte heap overflow), says Rails and classic-style Sinatra are exposed without authentication in their default configuration and plans to publish a code-execution proof of concept on stock Rails on 25 November 2026; no exploitation is reported. Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end of life, and the interpreter itself, not a gem, must be updated.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-132825NATOA2

Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14: seven memory-safety flaws in the regexp engine and string case conversion, three rated Critical by the project, with proofs of concept for code execution; Veria Labs says Rails and classic Sinatra are exposed by default and announces a public Rails exploit for 25 November 2026 (CVE-2026-132825, CVSS 3.1 7.4)

The Ruby project released 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 on 2026-11-18 to fix seven vulnerabilities in the regexp engine and in string case conversion, and says it is aware of proofs of concept that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution (Ruby project, 2026-11-18). NCSC.ch lists three as Critical, a one-byte heap overflow in case conversion of strings in single-byte encodings such as ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252, a double free in regexp compilation and a heap overflow from an integer overflow in regexp compilation, and the rest as High or Moderate (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19); the project's advisory for the first confirms it can write one byte past the output buffer (Ruby project, 2026-11-18). Most regexp flaws need an application that compiles, matches or stringifies an attacker-controlled pattern, and one needs only a crafted subject string against a fixed case-insensitive backreference pattern; the case-conversion flaw needs attacker-controlled text passed to a case-changing method (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19). Affected are Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 to 3.4.12 and 4.0.0 to 4.0.9, and Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end of life and unfixed (Ruby project, 2026-11-18).

NCSC.ch and watchTowr say Rails and classic-style Sinatra are exposed to the case-conversion overflow in their default configuration, and watchTowr reports no exploitation as of 2026-11-19 (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19; watchTowr, 2026-11-19). Veria Labs, which says it found the flaw independently and first demonstrated code execution, calls it Ruby2Shell, says it is reachable without authentication on Rails and classic Sinatra and that plain Rack and other frameworks are not exposed by default, and plans to publish a proof of concept for remote code execution on stock Rails on 25 November 2026, or later if major vendors have not shipped a fix (Veria Labs, 2026-11-20). Veria lists GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 and earlier and Chatwoot 4.20.0 and earlier as having no fixed release, and GitLab (fixed in 19.6.1, 19.5.8 and 19.4.10), Mastodon, OpenProject and the Discourse base image as patched; the Ruby advisories name no product, so the vendors' own advisories decide for each (Veria Labs, 2026-11-20). CVE-2026-132825 names the case-conversion overflow and is scored CVSS 3.1 7.4 with a local attack vector and high complexity (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-19); the Ruby announcement says CVE identifiers were requested and none was assigned at publication, so the other six flaws are known by GHSA id (Ruby project, 2026-11-18).

Exposure
Ruby 3.3, 3.4 and 4.0 below the fixed releases that run Rails or classic Sinatra, or any application that passes untrusted text to a case-changing method or compiles untrusted regexp patterns; the interpreter version is shown by ruby -v, and self-hosted products that bundle Ruby carry their own fix timeline (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19).
Detection
Crashes, segmentation faults and abnormal restarts of Ruby application workers that coincide with requests carrying long single-byte-encoded text or unusual regexp parameters, and a shell or network tool spawned by a Ruby worker process; these follow from the memory-corruption mechanism, as no source gives detection guidance.
Defender takeaway
Update the interpreter, not the gems, rebuild container images and restart workers before the announced proof of concept; until then NCSC.ch's temporary measures are to avoid compiling regexps from untrusted input and, for the case-conversion flaw, to convert input to UTF-8 so the vulnerable path is not reached (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19).

item.title: PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36: FPM request smuggling to code execution; the open session flaw is fixed
item.description: The PHP project released 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and 8.6.0 on 2026-11-19 with fixes for up to 18 CVEs per branch. The most direct is CVE-2026-129289: PHP-FPM keeps unread php://input bytes on a persistent FastCGI connection, so an unauthenticated multipart request can plant a second FastCGI request and run PHP code as the worker, but only behind a front end that reuses FastCGI connections, which standard nginx and Apache setups do not. The release also fixes CVE-2026-115560, left open in October, and follow-ups to an incomplete earlier fix; no source reports exploitation or a public proof of concept.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-129289 +7NATOA2

PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 and 8.2.36: CVE-2026-129289 lets an unauthenticated request smuggle a second FastCGI request into PHP-FPM and run PHP code when the front end reuses FastCGI connections; the release also fixes the session flaw left open in October and follow-ups to an incomplete earlier fix (CVSS 4.0 9.2)

The PHP project released 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and 8.6.0 on 2026-11-19, and the changelogs list up to 18 CVEs per branch (PHP, 2026-11-19). The most direct is CVE-2026-129289: when php://input was opened but not read to the end, PHP-FPM leaves the unread request bytes on a persistent FastCGI connection, so a malformed multipart body can place a second FastCGI request inside the first, and an unauthenticated attacker can bypass front-end routing and execute attacker-controlled PHP code with the privileges of the worker (PHP, 2026-11-19). It requires a front end that enables persistent backend connections and an application path that opens php://input without reading it fully; standard nginx and Apache configurations that close the FastCGI connection after each request are not affected by the demonstrated attack (PHP, 2026-11-19).

Two session flaws close the item the October release left open (watchTowr, 2026-11-20): CVE-2026-115560, where upload-progress session data is written in one serializer format and read in another, and CVE-2026-126714, where an interrupted write by the default files handler leaves a mixed old and new session file; both end in object injection and need an object gadget chain in the application (PHP, 2026-11-19; PHP, 2026-11-19). The fix for the first disables upload progress by default (PHP, 2026-11-19). CVE-2026-129481, a use-after-free of a stale session filename after an interrupted session shutdown, is in PHP's words an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619 and affects PHP 8.3 and later, and CVE-2026-129182, for PHP 8.5 only, covers further scenarios after the 8.5.12 fix (PHP, 2026-11-19; PHP, 2026-11-19).

CVE-2026-129474, PHP 8.5 only, is exposed on the built-in defaults, because fatal error backtraces are on in 8.5 and the default includes arguments, and php.ini-production, which sets zend.exception_ignore_args=1, or fatal_error_backtraces=0 prevents the attack; PHP confirmed code execution on 8.5 (PHP, 2026-11-19). CVE-2026-129496 needs a startup diagnostic written through a file-based error_log in a non-thread-safe build (PHP, 2026-11-19). CVE-2026-129291, an epoll use-after-free in PHP-FPM, gives root from a worker where catch_workers_output is on and the FPM master runs as root (PHP, 2026-11-19). NCSC.ch lists exploitation as unknown with no public proof of concept referenced, and watchTowr reports none as of 2026-11-20 (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19; watchTowr, 2026-11-20).

Exposure
PHP 8.5 without php.ini-production settings is exposed to CVE-2026-129474 on the defaults, when an application path enters a magic method (PHP, 2026-11-19). For CVE-2026-129289, PHP-FPM servers whose front end keeps FastCGI backend connections open (nginx fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi enablereuse=on, HAProxy in FastCGI mode) and whose applications open php://input without consuming it, which the PHP advisory says some frameworks do; standard nginx and Apache setups are outside the demonstrated attack (PHP, 2026-11-19). The session flaws need an object gadget chain in the application, and the version is shown by php -v on the host or in the container image.
Detection
In web and proxy access logs, malformed multipart/form-data bodies sent to endpoints whose application opens php://input without consuming it, followed by PHP execution that no logged request explains; in process telemetry, a shell or network tool spawned by the PHP-FPM worker, which follows from worker-level code execution.
Defender takeaway
Move the PHP runtime, not the CMS or its plugins, to the fixed build of its branch and restart PHP-FPM; where that waits, turn FastCGI connection reuse off (PHP, 2026-11-19). PHP 8.1 hosts need a newer branch for CVE-2026-129291 (PHP, 2026-11-19).

item.title: vCenter auth bypass exploited since September (GTIG), no workaround: update to 8.0 U3m, 9.0.2.0200 or 9.1.1.0200
item.description: Broadcom's advisory VMSA-2026-0009 of 2026-11-19 fixes CVE-2026-123890, an authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service of vCenter that needs only network access to vCenter (CVSS 3.1 9.8), with no workaround and, in Broadcom's words, an emergency change. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant say ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus actor, exploited it from early September 2026 to move from a compromised remote-support appliance to vCenter, forge administrator SAML sessions and extract domain-controller data from guest virtual disks on ESXi; Broadcom's advisory does not state exploitation. Fixed builds are 8.0 U3m, 9.0.2.0200, 9.1.1.0200 and VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2.5, and vCenter 7.0 has no public fix.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-123890 +4exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-123890, VMware vCenter Server: an unauthenticated authentication bypass in the Directory Service gives an administrator session; GTIG reports the suspected China-nexus actor ARMORY CASTLE exploited it from early September, Broadcom lists no workaround; fixed in 8.0 U3m, 9.0.2.0200 and 9.1.1.0200 (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

Broadcom's advisory VMSA-2026-0009 of 2026-11-19 fixes CVE-2026-123890, an authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service of vCenter: an actor with network access can bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access without credentials (CVSS 3.1 9.8) (Broadcom, 2026-11-19). Broadcom lists no workaround, calls the issue an emergency change and does not state exploitation (Broadcom, 2026-11-19). Broadcom credits Mandiant with the report (Broadcom, 2026-11-19), and Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant say ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus actor, exploited it in early September 2026 with its BONESAW utility, according to forensic evidence (GTIG, 2026-11-19). GTIG describes one intrusion that reached an internal vCenter from a Remote Support appliance compromised through the earlier BeyondTrust zero-day and names no victim sector or country (GTIG, 2026-11-19); BleepingComputer notes that Broadcom has not confirmed the exploitation (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-19).

The flaw is a session-key disclosure over DCE/RPC in the rpc_srp_verifier service on TCP 2012 that yields an authenticated administrator@vsphere.local session; BONESAW then read the Directory Service database, extracted the SAML signing key and created an SSO administrator, SAWSNAKE forged administrator SAML assertions, and the actor switched SSH on through the appliance management API, took the master symmetric key and the PostgreSQL credential file, switched SSH off again, logged in to ESXi hosts, planted an authorized_keys entry and extracted the domain database, registry hives and DNS data from Windows guest virtual disks before copying an archive out over SCP (GTIG, 2026-11-19).

Broadcom's response matrix names the fixes: vCenter 9.1 in 9.1.1.0200, 9.0 in 9.0.2.0200, 8.0 in 8.0 U3m, VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x in 5.2.5 through KB88287 and Telco Cloud through KB463116; vCenter 7.0 has no public fix, and extended-support customers contact Broadcom Support (Broadcom, 2026-11-19). The 8.0 U3m and 9.0.2.0200 updates block later upgrades to VCF 9.1.1 until 9.1.2 (Broadcom, 2026-11-19).

Exposure
VCenter 7.0, 8.0, 9.0 and 9.1 before the fixed builds; the only stated prerequisite is network access to vCenter, and GTIG's actor reached it from an internal Linux appliance, so exposure does not require an internet-facing vCenter (Broadcom, 2026-11-19; GTIG, 2026-11-19). The running build is in the vSphere Client Summary tab or in PowerCLI (Broadcom, 2026-11-19).
Detection
In the vCenter appliance management audit log, SSH switched on and then off again, a new local or SSO administrator, and reads of the Directory Service database, the master key and the PostgreSQL credential file; in network telemetry, sweeps of ports 2012, 5480 and 9080 from a Linux appliance that is not a management host; on ESXi, logins as vpxuser or root, a new authorized_keys entry and a hidden directory on a VMFS volume (GTIG, 2026-11-19). GTIG advises hardening the vCenter appliance beyond patching, and because BONESAW extracts the SAML signing key and the actor created accounts, the compromise check covers SSO and local administrators, signing material and ESXi keys from early September on (GTIG, 2026-11-19).

Triage: SSH enablement through the management API alone does not identify this activity; in GTIG's case it followed internal port sweeps from a non-management appliance and was reversed after the credential reads (GTIG, 2026-11-19).

Defender takeaway
Treat the update as an emergency change and plan around vCenter 7.0, which has no public fix; until it is in, GTIG's hardening guidance lists dropping inbound TCP 2012 from non-allowlisted addresses, to be tested first because the port carries SSO traffic (GTIG, 2026-11-19; Broadcom, 2026-11-19).

item.title: Mandiant: COLD RELIC turns one cloud compromise into the pretext for the next; enrolled passkeys outlive password resets
item.description: Mandiant reports that COLD RELIC, the name Google Threat Intelligence Group now uses for the group formerly tracked as COLDRIVER and UNC4057 (Star Blizzard), reused the staff directory and identities stolen from one US organisation in late 2025 to impersonate a contact when approaching a second in 2026. In the late-2025 case it took over a Super Admin account through push-notification fatigue, kept access with enrolled passkeys, MFA backup codes and rogue MFA devices that survived password and session resets, and exported the whole tenant; in 2026 it phished Entra ID credentials and registered a new MFA device to download one user's drive. GTIG names government officials, defense contractors and NGOs in Europe and North America as targets and says new phishing operations continued into November 2026.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

COLD RELIC: Mandiant shows the FSB-linked group reusing data stolen from one US organisation as the impersonation pretext for the next, then holding cloud tenants through MFA push fatigue and enrolled passkeys, backup codes and MFA devices that survive password and session resets

Mandiant reports a series of linked intrusions in which COLD RELIC, the name Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) now uses for the group formerly tracked as COLDRIVER and UNC4057 (also Star Blizzard, Callisto and Gossamer Bear), turned data stolen in one US organisation into the pretext for the next (GTIG, 2026-11-17). GTIG cites a US Department of Justice assessment that the group operates within Russia's FSB and names government officials, defense contractors and NGOs in Europe and North America among its targets (GTIG, 2026-11-17). In 2026 the operators approached a second US organisation over an encrypted messaging app while impersonating an employee of the first, shared phishing links that stole Entra ID credentials and tokens and sent the victim on to document lures matching the conversation, and registered a new MFA device on the account (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

In the late-2025 case the operators used the stolen credentials of a Super Admin account from a US residential proxy network close to the victim, pressed the user with MFA push notifications until one was accepted, registered a device model new to the tenant and kept access with passkeys, MFA backup codes and rogue MFA devices (GTIG, 2026-11-17). They took the whole cloud drive by mass sharing to an operator-run mailbox and by direct download, queried the admin investigation and email audit logs to check defensive visibility, viewed, modified and deleted Alert Center notifications, exported the employee list and ran a tenant-wide Customer Takeout export (GTIG, 2026-11-17). Access lasted several months through OAuth mail sync to an external client and re-authentication with enrolled passkeys that survived password and session resets, and in one case a password reset without revoking sessions did not evict the operators (GTIG, 2026-11-17). They searched for credentials, personnel data and .pst archives (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

Exposure
Google Workspace tenants, and Entra ID tenants that federate sign-in to Workspace as in the second case, whose privileged or staff accounts accept push, SMS or voice MFA or let users enrol passkeys, backup codes and devices without a second approval (GTIG, 2026-11-17).
Detection
In authentication logs, repeated failed logins or MFA challenges followed by a success from the same address, privileged sign-ins from residential-proxy networks that geolocate near the user, logins with a backup code, and new passkey or device registrations. In administrator audit logs, Customer Takeout creation, user-list downloads, audit-log investigation queries and Alert Center batch deletions. In Drive and OAuth logs, download spikes, external sharing to free mail providers, and authorisations of broad mail scopes to unapproved clients such as Thunderbird or Proton (GTIG, 2026-11-17). After a compromise, password changes alone are insufficient: revoke all sessions, refresh tokens and third-party OAuth permissions and remove unauthorised passkeys, backup codes and MFA devices (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

Triage: a directory export, a Customer Takeout or a passkey or device enrolment by an administrator can be routine; the cues in GTIG's account are an unfamiliar device, a non-corporate or residential-proxy network, or an enrolment right after an MFA-fatigue pattern (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

Defender takeaway
Move administrators and exposed staff to FIDO2 or WebAuthn hardware keys, which GTIG says cannot be approved through fatigue or intercepted by reverse proxies, require existing-administrator or out-of-band approval for new MFA devices and passkeys, and write session and OAuth revocation into compromise playbooks (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

item.title: BundID: mass automated logins lock citizen accounts; BSI confirms; password sign-in cut on 16 November
item.description: On 2026-11-16 Germany's BSI confirmed automated, mass login attempts against BundID, the federal citizen account for online administrative services: failed attempts locked accounts and triggered password-reset mails, and the federal government switched off username-and-password sign-in while eID and other sign-in means stayed open. The BSI has no indication that any account was compromised; Handelsblatt, citing government circles, calls it credential stuffing, and no Swiss portal is reported affected.
item.content:encoded:
ROUTINENATOB2

BundID: automated mass login attempts against Germany's federal citizen accounts lock accounts; the BSI confirms the attack, password sign-in was switched off on 16 November and no compromise is evidenced

Germany's BSI confirmed to heise security and Handelsblatt on 2026-11-16 an IT security incident involving BundID accounts: automated, mass login attempts whose failures locked accounts, triggered automated mails and prompted account holders to reset their passwords (heise, 2026-11-16). The federal government switched off username-and-password sign-in on Monday morning for security reasons (Handelsblatt, 2026-11-16), while sign-in with the online ID card (eID) and the Elster certificate stayed possible (WEB.DE, 2026-11-16). The BSI says countermeasures it does not name repelled the attack and that it has no indication of a compromise of any account, and heise reports that locked accounts are apparently not being unlocked in bulk, so account holders must pass the password-reset flow or use another sign-in method (heise, 2026-11-16). Handelsblatt, citing government circles, describes the attack as credential stuffing, the automated replay of credentials from earlier leaks at other services (Handelsblatt, 2026-11-16). An aggregator reports that password sign-in returned the same afternoon behind a mandatory e-mail one-time code (ad-hoc-news.de, 2026-11-16); no primary source read confirms it. The same aggregator attributes the credential-stuffing label to the BSI, which neither heise nor Handelsblatt does (ad-hoc-news.de, 2026-11-16). No Swiss portal is reported affected.

Exposure
Citizen-facing or employee-facing login portals that accept a password and lock an account after repeated failures.
Detection
Authentication logs showing a surge of failed password sign-ins spread over many usernames and sources, followed by lockout notices, password-reset mail volume and helpdesk contacts; a lockout storm is itself the alert.
Defender takeaway
The operator's containment, as heise and Handelsblatt report it, was to switch off the password-only path while eID and other sign-in means stayed open; a lockout-after-failures control turns credential stuffing into mass lockouts and reset mail even when no account is taken over, so settle that containment lever for your own portals before a run starts.

item.title: Unit 42: TGR-STA-0049 uses QUIC C2, logon-script spread and Exchange FullAccess loops against governments
item.description: Unit 42 reports that TGR-STA-0049 (also tracked as REF7707, Earth Alux and Ink Dragon) has attacked Southeast Asian government entities since at least July 2025, entering through unpatched Exchange and web servers, and says the group's targeting also includes governments in South America and Europe. Its new PerfectPioneer and KUKURAT implants use HTTP/3 over QUIC as the main command channel in most variants, the operators spread KUKURAT through domain logon scripts after taking a domain controller, and on Exchange they grant a compromised account FullAccess on every mailbox.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

TGR-STA-0049: Unit 42 describes the PerfectPioneer and KUKURAT implants, which use HTTP/3 over QUIC for command and control against government networks entered through unpatched Exchange servers, then spread through domain logon scripts and grant FullAccess on every mailbox

Unit 42 describes a campaign by TGR-STA-0049, also tracked as REF7707, Earth Alux and Ink Dragon, against Southeast Asian government entities since at least July 2025, and says the group's targeting also includes government organizations in South America and Europe (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). Server exploitation is the primary entry: unpatched Microsoft Exchange and web servers receive web shells, among them variants of ASPXSpy, Godzilla, Bysunue.aspx and Suo5, while phishing with decoy PDFs from lookalike government domains is secondary (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). The implants are two previously undocumented families: the Go-based PerfectPioneer RAT, active since July 2025 and run through DLL side-loading of a modified legitimate executable, decoy installers or phishing, and its modular C++ successor KUKURAT, deployed since March 2026, which loads at least 12 DLL modules from the command server into memory (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). Unit 42 says both families use HTTP/3 over QUIC as the primary command channel, with an automatic HTTP/2 fallback in the PerfectPioneer variant it analyzes, separate HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 builds of KUKURAT, and two PerfectPioneer variants, RatAAkk-tt and PerfectRat, that rely on HTTP/2 alone, and that some firewalls and inspection engines handle QUIC less well than TCP traffic (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). Two of the six PerfectPioneer variants, Pioneer and rat_http3_cc, carry a built-in blocklist that stops operators running noisy or destructive commands, and KUKURAT generates synthetic network, registry and file activity as camouflage (Unit 42, 2026-11-16).

After taking a domain controller, the operators installed malicious domain logon scripts, so each user's logon pulled KUKURAT; they also used PsExec, WMI and WinRM (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). Credentials came from LSASS dumps taken with rundll32 calling comsvcs.dll by ordinal rather than by the MiniDump name, from DCSync, and from Mimikatz, ProcDump, SharpDPAPI and SAM and SYSTEM hive dumps (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). On Exchange, the operators first listed accounts holding the ApplicationImpersonation role and, when none was found, ran a hidden PowerShell loop that granted a compromised account FullAccess on every mailbox (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). The exfiltration targeted pdf, docx, xlsx and png files whose names suggest international relations and internal political affairs (Unit 42, 2026-11-16).

Exposure
On-premises Exchange and other web servers that are unpatched and internet-facing, and Active Directory domains in which an attacker with domain controller access can edit logon scripts in SYSVOL or Group Policy.
Detection
Egress telemetry for outbound UDP 443 (QUIC) from servers that do not browse, since Unit 42 advises logging or blocking it so traffic falls back to TCP, paired with proxy and TLS egress telemetry because the HTTP/2-only variants and the KUKURAT HTTP/2 build never use UDP 443; SYSVOL and Group Policy change audit plus endpoint alerts on an uncommon startup process running under a domain user SID at logon, which raised an alert in Unit 42's telemetry; process events for rundll32 loading comsvcs.dll with an ordinal argument; and Exchange audit of ApplicationImpersonation role holders and of Add-MailboxPermission loops that grant FullAccess across all mailboxes (Unit 42, 2026-11-16).
Defender takeaway
Patch or isolate internet-facing Exchange and web servers first, then check domain logon scripts, ApplicationImpersonation holders and mailbox permissions, and decide whether servers need outbound UDP 443 at all.

item.description: Huntress confirmed exploitation of CVE-2026-84869 against MSP technicians: on 2026-11-12 a guest-pushed batch file ran on a technician's client with no prompt and installed a rogue ScreenConnect client within about nine seconds, while attacker guests were making 688,000 run-file requests on 42 MSP servers between 2026-10-20 and 2026-11-16. item.content:encoded:
Update17 Nov 2026 04:35 UTCrun 2026-11-17T0355Z-intelentitiessourcesevidenceactionsbodytitletechniques

Huntress confirmed exploitation of CVE-2026-84869 against MSP technicians: on 2026-11-12 a guest-pushed batch file ran on a technician's client with no prompt and installed a rogue ScreenConnect client within about nine seconds, while attacker guests were making 688,000 run-file requests on 42 MSP servers between 2026-10-20 and 2026-11-16. Updating the server does not fix it; every technician host client must be on 26.6.5 or later.

Huntress confirmed exploitation of CVE-2026-84869 against MSP technicians in a campaign it separates from the crypto-exchange-named decoy sessions it reported on 2026-11-13, and it describes the SCKit malware as appearing to leverage a vulnerable server-side extension, not to exploit this flaw directly (Huntress, 2026-11-16). On 2026-11-12 a technician at one MSP joined a blank-named Access session on the MSP's server and the host client ran a batch file the guest had pushed, with no prompt; within about nine seconds a hidden PowerShell relaunch, a curl download and an administrative-image unpack of an MSI ended with a rebranded ScreenConnect client connected to an attacker relay on port 8041 (Huntress, 2026-11-16). Huntress read the delivery side from server databases: between 2026-10-20 and 2026-11-16 attacker guests made 688,000 run-file requests for update.bat-style files from 29 source addresses on 42 MSP servers, repeating them in case a technician joined, and Huntress assesses with high confidence that the spray operator and the relay operator are the same (Huntress, 2026-11-16). In October an attacker also joined three real customer support sessions as an extra guest and asked the technician's client to run a path-traversal file into the Startup folder; two of the three technicians were on vulnerable Windows clients and the Mac client failed (Huntress, 2026-11-16).

The vulnerable code runs on the technician's machine, so updating the server alone does not close it, and Huntress saw many technicians on 22.x, 24.2 and 25.8 clients weeks after 26.6.5 shipped (Huntress, 2026-11-16). Server-side, Huntress points to guest-originated file-run events (RanFiles, EventType 85, or SentFiles, 86) in App_Data\Session.db, read from a copy, that overlap an open host connection; on workstations it points to the ScreenConnect client running batch or script files from its Temp folder, and to any client whose command line names a relay the organisation does not own (Huntress, 2026-11-16).

Open finding: CVE-2026-84869, ConnectWise ScreenConnect: a missing file-transfer authorization check lets an active remote session push and auto-run files on the Host, and Huntress traced worm-like exploitation back to 20 August, weeks before any patch existed (CVSS 9.9) →

It lists the observed steps (cloud-trust and vendor-credential pivots, Kudu abuse, Active Directory credential theft, exfiltration preparation), the telemetry to check and the attack-surface hardening it recommends.

The FBI's FLASH of 2026-11-13 (TLP:CLEAR) adds a US authority's account of ARTEX use. It says a variety of malicious actors have used the framework since at least August 2026 against organisations in financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications and legal services, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours (FBI, 2026-11-13). The original repository was withdrawn on 2026-10-08, but forks, archived copies and a commercial version keep the framework available, and researchers identified more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles in early November (FBI, 2026-11-13). The FBI says ARTEX excels at finding and exploiting peripheral systems that get less security attention: partner and supplier portals, mobile backends, employee applications, legacy services and third-party integrations (FBI, 2026-11-13).

The FBI's table of observed activity lists these further steps. Initial access came through unsigned SAML assertions, XXE, SSRF, anonymous file upload, hard-coded administrator passwords in single-page-application JavaScript bundles, stolen VPN configurations and leaked credentials, cross-account cloud trust abused from an external partner tenant, and compromised third-party vendor credentials used across trusted B2B federation. Persistence used JSP and PHP web shells (one route was MySQL log poisoning), Kudu administrative APIs to run commands, and credentials added to existing OAuth applications. For privilege escalation and internal discovery the agents used Kerberoasting, DCSync, resource-based constrained delegation abuse and a cloud metadata query through XXE, ran iterative PowerShell enumeration against domain controllers (over 110,000 Active Directory objects), read LAPS passwords and inventoried Windows hosts without a particular EDR sensor; attempted lateral movement to domain controllers by pass-the-ticket, WinRM, Kerberos relay and pass-the-hash was blocked by endpoint protection. Theft preparation used database queries, mass blob reads, custom boot scripts via EC2 instances and new 100 GB volumes, with command output sent to rotating webhook endpoints, and command and control ran through residential proxies, Tor, Chisel and SoftEther (FBI, 2026-11-13).

Telemetry the FBI lists: unexpected outbound calls to LLM API endpoints (to be read alongside other suspicious activity), high-frequency sequential enumeration against login and search endpoints, Azure Resource Manager deployment-validation dry runs across many resource types, IAM permission tests with DryRun flags and sub-second test blob writes and deletes, credential additions to applications and service principals in the Entra audit log, and .aspx or .jsp files in unexpected web-application paths (FBI, 2026-11-13). Its recommendations: inventory every internet-facing application including the peripheral ones named above, restrict Kudu/SCM endpoints, cloud administration, hypervisor and backup interfaces to trusted networks or dedicated administrative paths, and disable basic publishing authentication where it is not required. For every Microsoft 365 tenant where an affected ConnectWise application is or was authorised, it asks for a review by application ID of activity from at least 2026-10-01 and says not to delete the enterprise application before evidence is preserved (FBI, 2026-11-13).

Open finding: ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration →

item.title: Group-IB: DarkLunnen's FortiOS chain leaves a 'service' super_admin; Swiss FortiGates are scan targets only
item.description: Group-IB found an open directory on a Latvian server that documents more than 14 months of operations against Europe by an operator it tracks as DarkLunnen and links to no known actor: a modified public exploit for FortiOS CVE-2024-55591 that creates an administrator named service with super_admin privileges, among other tools. Group-IB recovered a list of 4,725 Swiss FortiGate scanning targets, which it says does not confirm vulnerability or exploitation, and restic commands that accessed an S3 backup repository at a Swiss domain in May and June 2025, without naming an organisation or confirming success.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLEexploitedNATOB2

DarkLunnen: Group-IB's exposed operator directory shows mass exploitation of FortiOS CVE-2024-55591 that plants a 'service' super_admin account, a 4,725-target Swiss FortiGate scan list and restic access to an S3 backup repository at a 'Swiss domain'; Group-IB does not confirm any Swiss victim

Group-IB reports that in late July 2026 it found an open directory on a Latvian server that held the operator's /root/ directory, 457 files of which 35 were recovered, and documents more than 14 months of operations against Europe by an operator it tracks as DarkLunnen; Group-IB links it to no known actor and does not establish nationality or state affiliation (Group-IB, 2026-11-11). The main campaign used a modified watchTowr proof of concept for FortiOS CVE-2024-55591, designed to create a backdoor super-admin account named service (Group-IB, 2026-11-11); the recovered results list about 600 devices in Turkey (hospitals, industry and municipalities), 16 in Ukraine, 14 in Azerbaijan and 1 in Algeria, and a stolen FortiGate configuration from a Romanian organisation carried the same account and yielded 10 cleartext VPN passwords (Group-IB, 2026-11-11).

The Swiss content is thin. Group-IB recovered a list of 4,725 FortiGate scanning targets for Switzerland and says such lists identify scanning targets but do not confirm vulnerability or successful exploitation; a table of additional operations also lists restic commands with AWS credentials accessing an S3 repository at a Swiss domain in May and June 2025, with production snapshots enumerated, and the report names no organisation and says that for several operations the evidence is limited to recorded commands (Group-IB, 2026-11-11). Fortinet's advisory FG-IR-24-535 lists FortiOS 7.0.0 through 7.0.16 and FortiProxy 7.2.0 through 7.2.12 and 7.0.0 through 7.0.19 as affected, fixed in 7.0.17, 7.2.13 and 7.0.20, names FortiOS 7.2, 7.4, 7.6 and 6.4 as not affected and offers disabling the HTTP/HTTPS administrative interface as the workaround (Fortinet PSIRT, 2025-01-14).

Exposure
A FortiOS 7.0 device below 7.0.17, or a FortiProxy below its fixed release, whose HTTP/HTTPS administrative interface was ever reachable from the internet; a device exposed while vulnerable can carry an account that patching does not remove (Group-IB, 2026-11-11).
Detection
In FortiGate event logs, an administrator named service with the super_admin profile, any unexplained administrator or local user, and super_admin logins or account creation through the jsconsole interface, which Fortinet lists among its indicators; in VPN logs, logins with accounts whose secrets sat in an exposed configuration (Group-IB, 2026-11-11).
Defender takeaway
Hunt for the account on patched devices too, assume the configuration was read on a device that was exposed while vulnerable and rotate the VPN user passwords, administrator passwords, IPsec pre-shared keys and LDAP or RADIUS credentials it stored, review VPN logs and enforce MFA, and enable private data encryption, which is off by default (Group-IB, 2026-11-11); no source says that a Swiss organisation was compromised.

item.title: WFX Phantom: stolen GitHub tokens push a CI stealer; cloud persistence meant to survive rotation; check for probe PRs
item.description: StepSecurity and Aikido report that from 2026-11-10 an attacker uses stolen GitHub tokens, not a GitHub Actions bug, to open probe pull requests titled "docs: dependency audit notes" and then push a stealer script into workflows, CI scripts or npm hooks where the token's permissions allow, taking Actions secrets, runner memory and cloud credentials, planting AWS and Azure persistence and deleting the workflow runs. Counts differ by lab and time (more than 63,000 probes; at least 1,835 repositories where the payload ran); how the tokens were obtained is unknown, and no Swiss victim is named.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB1

WFX Phantom: stolen GitHub tokens push a CI secret stealer into repositories from 2026-11-10, steal Actions secrets, runner memory and cloud tokens, plant AWS and Azure persistence designed to outlast rotation and delete the workflow runs; StepSecurity counts more than 63,000 probe pull requests

StepSecurity reports that from 2026-11-10 an attacker uses stolen GitHub tokens of real developer and bot accounts, as a developer would, not a bug in GitHub Actions, to push a CI secret stealer into repositories those tokens can write to (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12). It first opens a pull request titled "docs: dependency audit notes" from a branch named wfx-docs that only proves write access; StepSecurity counts more than 63,000 such probes by 2026-11-12 (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12), Aikido, which tracks the campaign as wfx-loot, counts 4,837 compromised accounts and at least 1,835 repositories where the payload ran, and Endor Labs counts 8,926 infected repositories (Aikido, 2026-11-12; Endor Labs, 2026-11-12); BleepingComputer reports that the compromised accounts included those of the US General Services Administration and the French government (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-12).

Where the token's permissions and the repository's setup let it run, the attacker pushes a script of about 1,500 lines through an edit to an existing workflow or CI shell script, a new workflow on a short-lived branch or a hidden script that an npm hook runs, and the script collects every Actions secret, the job token, the memory of the runner worker process and credential files for the major clouds and registries, then uses the job's OIDC token to open AWS, GCP and Azure sessions (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12). It plants persistence meant to outlast rotation, a rewritten AWS role trust policy with new access keys and federated identity credentials on Azure applications, sends the archive over HTTP and from 2026-11-12 through a Telegram bot, and within about a minute pushes a revert commit and deletes the workflow run, leaving a gap in the run numbers that StepSecurity calls the most reliable sign the stealer ran (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12). How the tokens were obtained is not known: some probes came through the Fly.io GitHub App, and StepSecurity has no evidence of a breach of Fly.io (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12). BleepingComputer's report of Aikido's findings gives the same probe title and start date (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-12).

Exposure
Any account or bot with write access to repositories you own or build from whose token may be exposed (a personal access token, an OAuth grant, a GitHub App user token), and any build with cloud OIDC trust or long-lived secrets; bots that bypass branch protection raise the risk (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12).
Detection
In source-control data, pull requests titled "docs: dependency audit notes", branches named wfx-docs and commits since 2026-11-10 with the messages "ci: refresh build cache", "ci: restore", "ci: cleanup", "chore: add ci helper" or "chore: add dependency audit workflow", and in CI run history a gap in the run numbers right after one; in AWS and Azure audit logs, changes to role trust policies, newly created access keys and federated credentials named wfx-ci (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12).

Triage: a probe pull request alone shows that the account that opened it is compromised, even if nothing else happened; the payload probably ran where a commit with one of those messages is paired with a deleted run (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12).

Defender takeaway
Treat the account behind any probe or payload commit as compromised and revoke its tokens; where the payload ran, rotation is not enough because the persistence is designed to outlast it, and Endor Labs says secrets rotated after the first wave were likely stolen again in 1,838 repositories (Endor Labs, 2026-11-12).

Builds on: GhostAction: fake security workflows now harvest whole git histories; rotating Actions secrets…

item.title: Unit 42: Falcon C2 runs inside the browser, fed by a script tag in government webmail such as Roundcube
item.description: Unit 42 describes Falcon, a NodeJS command-and-control framework whose JavaScript implant runs inside the victim's browser and leaves no file on the endpoint, planted by a script tag in government webmail portals and web applications, among them the Roundcube webmail of a Middle Eastern foreign ministry (39 instances in that country), and by a sideloaded Chrome extension disguised as a PDF viewer. Unit 42 saw it against government bodies in one Middle Eastern and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026, names no actor, does not say how the script tags were placed and is unaware how the extensions are deployed, and assesses with high confidence that Falcon and PeckBirdy are variants of one core framework.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Falcon: Unit 42 describes a browser-resident command-and-control framework planted in government webmail and web applications, with a script tag in Roundcube at a Middle Eastern foreign ministry and a sideloaded 'PDF Viewer' extension elsewhere; it shares its core with PeckBirdy

Unit 42 describes Falcon C2, also called XG and not the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor, a NodeJS command-and-control framework whose operator-controlled JavaScript implant runs inside the victim's browser, so the endpoint holds no file for it (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). A script tag placed in a trusted site makes each visit request the implant from the Falcon server, which returns a script obfuscated per browser session, and the implant then holds a TLS WebSocket to the server while the tab is open and runs operator JavaScript through eval (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). Unit 42 identified compromised government entities in one Middle Eastern and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026, among them ministries and law enforcement agencies, and names no actor (Unit 42, 2026-11-11).

In April 2026 a script tag inserted into the Roundcube webmail portal of a Middle Eastern ministry of foreign affairs let the operator intercept credentials as users signed in and monitor sessions (39 Roundcube instances in that country, none observed elsewhere; how the tag got in is not stated) (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). In May 2026 a module in a Southeast Asian police web application harvested usernames and then showed a fake Adobe Flash Player update prompt to chosen users, which served the Antino implant that uses Microsoft OneDrive for command and control (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). Against a justice-department entity in another country, a Chrome extension named PDF Viewer, sideloaded in developer mode, checked in every 3 to 4 minutes for over three weeks and exfiltrated plaintext credentials for an internal correspondence system and a screenshot of a document the victim was viewing (Unit 42, 2026-11-11). The Jewelbug campaign also used an extension named PDF Viewer (Symantec, 2026-08-13); Unit 42 lists it only as a further resource.

Unit 42 assesses with high confidence that Falcon and PeckBirdy (Trend's JScript framework used by China-aligned actors since 2023) are variants of one core framework; that is code lineage, not who operates Falcon (Unit 42, 2026-11-11; Trend Micro, 2026-01-26).

Exposure
Internal webmail, ticketing and case-management portals whose templates or headers an attacker can edit (Roundcube is the named case), and managed Chrome browsers that allow extensions to be sideloaded in developer mode; Unit 42 does not say how the script tags or the extensions reached their targets.
Detection
Unit 42's four monitoring items, telemetry class first: template and header integrity on webmail, ticketing and case-management portals for a script tag loading a resource from an unfamiliar domain, especially one returning a heavily numeric JavaScript array with a small decoder loop; extension inventory for developer-mode extensions imitating utilities such as PDF viewers with broad permissions; Baidu Analytics-style cookie or local-storage keys on internal government web applications; and OneDrive traffic to tenants outside the organisation's own with repeated small JSON writes (Unit 42, 2026-11-11).

Triage: Unit 42's basis for the cookie check is that Baidu Analytics cookies are normal on sites that use that service and anomalous on internal government web applications where it has no reason to appear (Unit 42, 2026-11-11).

Defender takeaway
Compare the templates and headers of internal webmail and case-management portals with a known-good copy and list every external script source they load, and inventory the Chrome extensions installed in developer mode on managed browsers; a browser-resident implant leaves nothing on the endpoint for file-based tools to find.

Update11 Nov 2026 03:54 UTCrun 2026-11-11T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidencebody

PK Softech and the State Secretariat for Security Policy said on 2026-11-10 that no concrete ransom demand reached the supplier or the federal bodies, that the supplier never contacted the attackers, that the Confederation paid nothing and that there is still no indication of publication on the darkweb, which qualifies the press report that Akira demands ransom.

PK Softech said on its homepage on 2026-11-10, "because of media speculation", that no concrete ransom demand has reached it and that it has at no time contacted the attackers; its investigation continues (PK Softech, 2026-11-10). A spokeswoman of the State Secretariat for Security Policy told Keystone-SDA the same day that the federal bodies handling the incident know of no concrete ransom demand addressed to them and that the Confederation paid no ransom, that, as she put it, a demand to the supplier was "not made concrete with an amount or deadline" (translated from German), and that the Secretariat still has no indication that data from the attack was published on the darkweb; Publica said it also received no demand, is not in contact with the hackers and does not know whether other organisations or individuals are being extorted, which the Federal Prosecutor's Office is investigating (watson.ch, 2026-11-10). This qualifies the press report that Akira demands ransom: watson.ch's headline and lead say no demand reached the supplier or the Confederation, while the spokeswoman's wording leaves a non-specific demand to the supplier open, and neither the supplier nor the federal authorities confirm a concrete demand, and the Akira attribution and the data volume remain press-sourced.

item.title: ESET: Turla's Cereal runs the victim's own Exchange server as C2 and wraps transport agents to collect mail
item.description: ESET found a previously undocumented .NET toolset, Cereal, on a Kazakh government organisation's Exchange server in November 2025 and on a Romanian government organisation's from December 2025, and attributes it to Turla with high confidence. The compromised Exchange server is the command channel, answering requests on web paths that imitate Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync, and a module injected into the transport service wraps existing transport agents to collect mail, in Romania configured to select messages to or from NATO and EU addresses; ESET could not determine the initial access method.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

Turla's Cereal toolset turns a compromised on-premises Exchange server into the command channel and mail collector at Kazakh and Romanian government bodies, with no attacker infrastructure and no new transport agent registered (ESET)

ESET found a previously undocumented .NET toolset, Cereal, on a Kazakh government organisation's Exchange server on 2025-11-28 and on a Romanian government organisation's Exchange server compromised from 2025-12-23; in Romania the mail-collection module was configured to identify messages to or from NATO and EU institutional addresses (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). ESET attributes Cereal to Turla with high confidence, on the concurrent use of another component publicly linked to Turla and conceptual similarity to older Turla malware, and could not determine the initial access method, although it considers a vulnerability exploit possible because the servers are reachable from the internet (ESET Research, 2026-11-10).

The command channel is the victim's own Exchange server. CerealNeuron runs on the compromised server and passively waits for requests on web paths made to look like Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync traffic; a correctly encrypted request is treated as a command and a bad one gets a normal-looking Exchange error page, and ESET found no operator-controlled server and could not identify ingress addresses (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). Each task runs as a small .NET assembly inside a CerealRunner (mailbox retrieval, Active Directory and WMI queries, LSA secrets extraction, file operations) (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). CerealLoader, the only component written to disk in recognisable .NET form, abuses .NET VTable fixups so native code runs before managed code and is placed where trusted processes load it: the System32 wbem directory (ncobjapi.dll, wbemcomn.dll, loaded by WMI) and the .NET native image cache (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). CerealBox, injected into EdgeTransport.exe, wraps the handlers of transport agents already loaded, so "no new agent appears anywhere in Exchange's configuration"; it keeps messages with .doc, .docx or .pdf attachments that match hard-coded sender, recipient, subject or attachment-name lists and stages them compressed and encrypted on disk for exfiltration through CerealNeuron (ESET Research, 2026-11-10).

Exposure
Any organisation that runs Microsoft Exchange on premises with a role reachable from the internet; ESET names no vulnerable version, so exposure is the deployment model.
Detection
File-integrity telemetry on the Exchange host for DLLs in the System32 wbem directory and .NET native image cache files that do not match the Microsoft originals; module telemetry for non-Microsoft assemblies loaded into EdgeTransport.exe while Get-TransportAgent lists nothing new; web-server logs for requests to the Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync look-alike paths from clients with no matching mailbox flow, whose encrypted bodies return a generic error page; and Exchange Web Services mailbox retrievals made from the server's own context. ReversingLabs adds live HTTP.sys listeners (netsh http show servicestate) and proxy, load-balancer and WAF logs for the look-alike paths, proxy DLLs that mimic system libraries in the service directories, and module loads in WmiPrvSE.exe (ReversingLabs, 2026-11-19). With no external C2 and no known entry vector, the check is a compromise assessment of every internet-facing Exchange server.

Triage: third-party anti-spam, data-loss-prevention and archiving products also inject into the transport service, but they are vendor-signed and appear in the transport-agent configuration, which CerealBox does not; the native image cache regenerates legitimately after .NET updates, so only a file that does not match the Microsoft binary is the signal.

Defender takeaway
Treat internet-facing Exchange servers as top-tier assets, baseline the wbem directory and the native image cache, and run the compromise assessment now, because network-only detection will not find a channel that rides the victim's own web paths.
Improvement20 Nov 2026 05:12 UTCrun 2026-11-20T0356Z-intelsourcesbody

ReversingLabs correlated ESET's published loader samples and says the same files carry different vendor names, CerealLoader at ESET, BlankPage in Microsoft Defender and CerealMood in other engines, so a hunt on a single family name can miss matches; it says the work extends the artifacts defenders can search for and establishes no additional victims or initial-access method (ReversingLabs, 2026-11-19). Its hunting guidance (HTTP.sys listeners, proxy-DLL loaders such as version.dll and WTSAPI32.dll, and WmiPrvSE.exe module loads) is in the Detection line (ReversingLabs, 2026-11-19).
